name: Yolanda Ibarra
languages: German (the school insisted, and the folklore journals are in it)
equipment: Silver knife: a sterling fruit knife from her mother's good set, which she took for luck and her mother does not know is missing
A few good books: a German folklore dictionary, a field guide to Wisconsin birds, a paperback of Midwestern ghost stories she is embarrassed to own
Notebook and pencil, three of each
Library card: State Historical Society of Wisconsin, stamped READER
A letter of enrollment from the Folklore Program, University of Wisconsin, and a letter of introduction from her advisor 'to whom it may concern'
Tape recorder: a Panasonic cassette recorder and six blank tapes, for interviews

Photostats: the Hollow Fork Furrow for 1926 and 1938 ('the old custom of the harvest kerchief'; 'every traveler welcome at our table'), and a page from the 1938 WPA folklore survey of Kinnick County: 'Saying, recorded over the ridge: Don't eat at the Fork in the fall'
A bag of oddments for The Right Things in the Bag: candles, chalk, red thread, a bell, a pinch of salt, iron nails, a sprig of rue
A coat that is not warm enough
features: Seen It in a Book (Educated origin: once per long rest she recalls one useful fact about history, science, law, geography or a book she has read without a check; advantage on Research checks in a library, archive or registry; she reads old handwriting, Latin inscriptions and legal language without a check)

Old Lore (Occultist: once the party has seen a creature or clear sign of it, she can spend an action and make an INT (Occult) check, DC 10 + the creature's CR; on a success the GM tells her one of its rules the party has not yet learned; once per creature per long rest. She has advantage on Occult checks to perform a rite or set a ward, and performs them in half the usual time)
The Right Things in the Bag (Occultist: once per scenario, when a rite or ward needs a common object she could plausibly have packed, a candle, a nail, red thread, a bell, chalk, she has it)
Steeped in It (Occultist, 2nd level: advantage on fear checks against the sign of a horror; whenever she or the party learn one of a creature's rules, she loses 1 Dread)
Tradition: Folklorist (Occultist, 3rd level: advantage on Persuasion checks with the old, and an interview with the oldest person in a place always yields one true clue toward a creature's rule)

Library Privileges (Student background: she can get into any academic library and many private ones, a professor will usually see her about their subject, and other students will put her up for a night; people explain things to her in more detail than they would to anyone else)
traits: The Right Things in the Bag (1/scenario)

personality.traits: I ask old people questions and then actually listen to the answers. I take notes on everything, including conversations I am in. I get excited about the wrong things at the wrong moments.
personality.ideals: Folklore is what people know that nobody wrote down. Somebody should write it down, and then believe it.
personality.bonds: My mother and grandmother in Milwaukee, who think a doctorate in folklore is a doctorate in fairy tales and are proud of me anyway. My advisor, who said Hollow Fork would make my dissertation. Mrs. Jean Hovland, the Linden Falls librarian, whose letter told me about the kerchiefs.
personality.flaws: I want this to be real so badly that I will walk toward it when I should be walking away.

appearance: Twenty-seven, small, round-faced and bright-eyed, with long black hair in a braid, big tortoiseshell glasses, a corduroy jacket with patched elbows, a coat that is not warm enough, and a cassette recorder on a strap over her shoulder.
backstory: Yolanda Ibarra grew up on the south side of Milwaukee, above her father's barbershop on National Avenue, the first in her family to finish high school, then college, then a master's degree; she is now a doctoral candidate in the Folklore Program at Madison, writing a dissertation on harvest customs in the Upper Midwest: last-sheaf rites, harvest suppers, threshing-crew songs, the things that German, Norwegian, Czech and Polish farm families brought or invented and their grandchildren have half forgotten. In the State Historical Society's microfilm she kept finding Hollow Fork: a 1926 Furrow piece on 'the old custom of the harvest kerchief', worn in no other town she can find; a 1938 piece about the Harvest Supper, 'every traveler welcome at our table'; and in the 1938 WPA folklore survey of Kinnick County, a saying recorded over the ridge, 'Don't eat at the Fork in the fall.' She wrote to the county librarian, who wrote back three pages. She has booked a room at the Harvest Moon for the seventieth Harvest Days. (Hook: the story, a scholar's. She has not yet read the 1904 Furrow; that is in hs-scenario-002, and she knows exactly which reel to ask for.)
